hints: Start by drawing trichloroethene, $\text{CHCl=CCl}_2$, and remember addition across the C=C breaks the double bond to give a saturated product.
Recall a carbon is chiral when it has four different groups attached, so check each new saturated carbon after addition.
Test each reagent by adding its two parts across the double bond, then see which product creates a carbon with H, Cl, Br and a carbon chain all at once.
walkthrough:
**Draw the starting alkene**

Think of trichloroethene as an ethene with three H atoms replaced by Cl.

Chemical structure:
$$\text{CHCl=CCl}_2$$

**Recall what makes a product chiral**

A molecule is chiral if it has a carbon with four different groups attached and no plane of symmetry.

Chirality rule:
$$\text{chiral C = C attached to 4 different atoms/groups}$$

**Add bromine across the double bond**

Bromine undergoes electrophilic addition, one Br adds to each carbon of the C=C.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{CHCl=CCl}_2 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CHBrCl-CBrCl}_2$$

**Check for a chiral centre**

Look at the left carbon in the product. It is bonded to H, Cl, Br and $\text{CBrCl}_2$.

That is four different groups, so it is a chiral centre and the product is chiral as a racemic mixture.

options.A: Addition of $\text{Br}_2$ gives $\text{CHBrCl-CBrCl}_2$. The first carbon is attached to H, Br, Cl and $\text{CBrCl}_2$, four different groups, so it is a chiral centre. The product is formed as a racemate and is chiral.
options.B: Addition of HCl gives a tetrachloroethane, either $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl-CCl}_3$ or $\text{CHCl}_2\text{-CHCl}_2$. In both cases each carbon has at least two identical substituents (two H or two/three Cl), so no carbon has four different groups and the product is achiral.
options.C: Cyanide ion does not undergo simple addition to this electron-poor chloroalkene under normal conditions to give a saturated chiral nitrile. Students may confuse this with HCN addition to carbonyls, but alkenes do not react this way with NaCN.
options.D: NaOH can cause elimination or substitution of the chloroalkene, but it does not add two different groups across the double bond to create a carbon with four different substituents. The products formed are unsaturated or achiral, not chiral.
